title: Building Boxes
statement:
A storeroom is a cube whose width, length and height all equal `n`. You must put `n` unit cubes (boxes) inside it under two rules:

- a box may stand anywhere on the floor;
- a box may rest on top of another box `y` only if each of the four vertical faces of `y` touches either a neighbouring box or a wall of the room.

Return the smallest possible number of boxes standing on the floor.
notes:
## Intuition

Walls count as support, so boxes belong in a corner. The best full shape there is a staircase pyramid: with `size` diagonals on the floor it has `size(size+1)/2` floor boxes and `1 + 3 + 6 + ... = size(size+1)(size+2)/6` boxes in all, and growing it by one diagonal adds a whole triangle of `(size+1)(size+2)/2` boxes. Once no further full triangle fits, put floor boxes one by one along the next diagonal, starting at a wall: the 1st adds 1 box, the 2nd lets one more box sit on the old pyramid (2 in total), the `j`-th adds `j`. Taking the largest pyramid first and then the cheapest extra floor boxes is greedy and optimal. Trying every floor count and simulating the stacking also works, but only for small `n`.

## Approach

1. Grow `size` while the next triangle still fits: `used + (size+1)(size+2)/2 <= n`; add that triangle to `used`.
2. The pyramid's floor holds `floor = size(size+1)/2` boxes.
3. While `used < n`, add one floor box: `extra` goes up by 1 and `used` grows by `extra`.
4. Return `floor + extra`.

## Example 1, step by step

`n = 3`. The first triangle (1 box) fits: `size = 1`, `used = 1`. The next needs 3 more, giving 4 > 3, so the pyramid stops with `floor = 1`. The first extra floor box makes `used = 2`, the second makes `used = 4 >= 3`, so `extra = 2` and the answer is `1 + 2 = 3`.

## Complexity

- Time: O(n^(1/3)): `size` grows to about the cube root of `6n` (1816 for `n = 10^9`) and `extra` stays at most `size + 1`.
- Space: O(1).

## Pitfalls

- Extra floor boxes are worth 1, 2, 3, ... boxes, not a full layer each.
- Stop growing the pyramid when the next triangle would exceed `n`; overshooting gives too many floor boxes.
- Return floor boxes, not the total number of boxes.
- A floating cube root can be off by one; the integer loops are exact.

## Variables

| Name | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `size` | number of floor diagonals in the full corner pyramid |
| `used` | boxes placed so far |
| `floor` | floor boxes of the full pyramid |
| `extra` | floor boxes added along the next diagonal |

narration.2: size counts the floor diagonals of the full pyramid in the corner.
narration.3: used counts every box placed so far.
narration.5: Growing the pyramid by one diagonal adds a triangle of (size+1)(size+2)/2 boxes; do it only if they all fit.
narration.6: The pyramid now has one more floor diagonal...
narration.7: ...and all boxes of the new triangle are placed.
narration.10: The full pyramid's floor is a triangle of size(size+1)/2 boxes.
narration.12: Some boxes remain, so add floor boxes along the next diagonal.
narration.14: ...lets extra boxes be placed in total: itself plus extra - 1 on top of the pyramid.
narration.16: The answer is the pyramid's floor plus the extra floor boxes.
